questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: Menopause is diagnosed clinically when a woman over 45 has had:
options: Twelve consecutive months of amenorrhoea with no other cause
Any hot flushes with irregular periods
A single raised follicle-stimulating hormone value
questions.concept: The diagnosis is retrospective and clinical in this age group, so hormone measurement is unnecessary and may mislead because gonadotropins fluctuate widely during the perimenopause.
questions.reference: Shaw's Textbook of Gynaecology 17e, Ch. Menopause

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman has amenorrhoea for a year with two follicle-stimulating hormone values above 25 IU/L taken 4 weeks apart. The diagnosis and key management principle are:
options: Premature ovarian insufficiency, requiring hormone replacement until the average age of menopause
questions.concept: Oestrogen replacement in premature ovarian insufficiency is not optional hormone therapy but replacement of a deficiency, protecting bone and cardiovascular health until about age 51.
questions.reference: Shaw's Textbook of Gynaecology 17e, Ch. Menopause

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: Which symptom of the menopause responds best to systemic oestrogen therapy?
questions.concept: Oestrogen reduces flush frequency by 75 percent or more and is the most effective treatment; genitourinary atrophy responds to local oestrogen and low libido may need androgen in addition.
questions.reference: Shaw's Textbook of Gynaecology 17e, Ch. Menopause

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A woman with an intact uterus is prescribed hormone therapy. Why must a progestogen be added to oestrogen?
options: To prevent endometrial hyperplasia and carcinoma from unopposed oestrogen
questions.concept: Unopposed oestrogen increases endometrial cancer risk severalfold, so a progestogen or the levonorgestrel intrauterine system is mandatory unless the woman has had a hysterectomy.
questions.reference: Shaw's Textbook of Gynaecology 17e, Ch. Menopause

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: Which route of oestrogen therapy carries the lowest risk of venous thromboembolism?
questions.concept: Avoiding first-pass hepatic metabolism means transdermal oestrogen has less effect on clotting factors and is preferred in women with obesity, migraine or a raised thrombotic risk.
questions.reference: Shaw's Textbook of Gynaecology 17e, Ch. Menopause

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: Which non-hormonal drug has the best evidence for reducing hot flushes in a woman with a history of breast cancer on tamoxifen?
questions.concept: Paroxetine and fluoxetine inhibit CYP2D6 and reduce conversion of tamoxifen to its active metabolite, so venlafaxine, gabapentin or clonidine are preferred, and systemic oestrogen is contraindicated.
questions.reference: Shaw's Textbook of Gynaecology 17e, Ch. Menopause

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A postmenopausal woman has a DXA T-score of minus 2.7 at the femoral neck with no fracture. First-line pharmacological treatment is:
options: An oral bisphosphonate with calcium and vitamin D
questions.concept: A T-score of minus 2.5 or below defines osteoporosis, and bisphosphonates reduce vertebral and hip fracture with the best cost-effectiveness; teriparatide is reserved for severe disease or bisphosphonate failure.
questions.reference: Shaw's Textbook of Gynaecology 17e, Ch. Menopause

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: Which finding would make a woman ineligible for menopausal hormone therapy?
options: Current or past oestrogen-receptor-positive breast cancer
questions.concept: Absolute contraindications include current or past hormone-dependent breast or endometrial cancer, active venous thromboembolism, undiagnosed vaginal bleeding and active liver disease.
questions.reference: Shaw's Textbook of Gynaecology 17e, Ch. Menopause

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: Why is hormone therapy started within 10 years of menopause associated with a different cardiovascular effect than therapy started later?
options: Oestrogen is protective on relatively healthy endothelium but may destabilise established atherosclerotic plaque
questions.concept: This timing hypothesis reconciles the Women's Health Initiative findings with observational data and underlies the current window-of-opportunity approach to prescribing.
questions.reference: Shaw's Textbook of Gynaecology 17e, Ch. Menopause

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: Which FIGO category describes abnormal uterine bleeding caused by a submucosal fibroid?
questions.concept: The PALM-COEIN system separates structural causes, polyp, adenomyosis, leiomyoma and malignancy, from non-structural ones, and submucosal fibroids are the subtype that most often causes heavy bleeding.
questions.reference: Shaw's Textbook of Gynaecology 17e, Ch. Disorders of Menstruation and Fibroids

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A 30-year-old with a 4 cm submucosal fibroid causing heavy bleeding wishes to preserve fertility. The best treatment is:
questions.concept: Submucosal fibroids distorting the cavity are removed transcervically with good improvement in bleeding and fertility, whereas embolisation is generally avoided in women planning pregnancy.
questions.reference: Shaw's Textbook of Gynaecology 17e, Ch. Disorders of Menstruation and Fibroids

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A woman with a rapidly enlarging uterine mass after the menopause with pain and a raised lactate dehydrogenase should be evaluated for:
questions.concept: Fibroids should regress after the menopause, so growth in a postmenopausal woman is a red flag; this is also why morcellation is avoided when sarcoma is suspected.
questions.reference: Shaw's Textbook of Gynaecology 17e, Ch. Disorders of Menstruation and Fibroids

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: Which diagnostic criterion set defines polycystic ovary syndrome, requiring two of three features?
options: Rotterdam criteria: oligo-ovulation, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovarian morphology
questions.concept: Because two of three features suffice, women may have the syndrome without cysts on ultrasound, and other causes of hyperandrogenism such as congenital adrenal hyperplasia must be excluded.
questions.reference: Shaw's Textbook of Gynaecology 17e, Ch. Disorders of Menstruation and Fibroids

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A woman with polycystic ovary syndrome and oligomenorrhoea who does not want pregnancy needs endometrial protection because:
options: Chronic anovulation exposes the endometrium to unopposed oestrogen, raising the risk of hyperplasia and carcinoma
Insulin resistance is carcinogenic to the cervix
questions.concept: Cyclical progestogen, a combined pill or the levonorgestrel intrauterine system induces regular shedding and reverses hyperplasia, and this is a core long-term management aim independent of fertility.
questions.reference: Shaw's Textbook of Gynaecology 17e, Ch. Disorders of Menstruation and Fibroids

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: Which ultrasound finding at 11 weeks establishes a monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy?
options: A T-sign at the intertwin membrane insertion with a single placental mass
The lambda or twin peak sign
questions.concept: Chorionicity is best determined in the first trimester, and the thin membrane inserting perpendicularly as a T marks monochorionicity, which carries all the specific complications of shared circulation.
questions.reference: DC Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics 9e, Ch. Multiple Pregnancy

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: Which complication is unique to monochorionic twins?
questions.concept: Vascular anastomoses in a shared placenta allow unbalanced transfusion, producing a donor with oligohydramnios and a recipient with polyhydramnios, which is why monochorionic pregnancies need fortnightly scans from 16 weeks.
questions.reference: DC Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics 9e, Ch. Multiple Pregnancy

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: Amniotic fluid index above 24 cm with a single deepest pocket over 8 cm defines:
questions.concept: Polyhydramnios raises the risk of preterm labour, malpresentation, cord prolapse and postpartum haemorrhage, and its causes include maternal diabetes, fetal swallowing defects and fetal anaemia.
questions.reference: DC Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics 9e, Ch. Multiple Pregnancy

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A monochorionic twin pair at 20 weeks has one twin with a deepest pocket of 1 cm and the other with 10 cm. The treatment of choice is:
options: Fetoscopic laser ablation of the placental anastomoses
questions.concept: The Eurofoetus trial showed better survival and neurological outcome with laser photocoagulation than amnioreduction for stage II and above twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome before 26 weeks.
questions.reference: DC Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics 9e, Ch. Multiple Pregnancy

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A fetus has an abdominal circumference below the third centile with a normal head circumference and normal umbilical artery Doppler. This pattern suggests:
options: Asymmetrical growth restriction from placental insufficiency, with brain sparing
A constitutionally small but healthy fetus
questions.concept: Late-onset placental insufficiency spares the head at the expense of the abdomen and subcutaneous fat, whereas early symmetrical restriction suggests an intrinsic fetal cause such as aneuploidy or infection.
questions.reference: DC Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics 9e, Ch. Multiple Pregnancy

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: Which measure has been shown to reduce the risk of preterm birth in a woman with a twin pregnancy and a short cervix?
options: Routine cervical cerclage in all twins
questions.concept: Meta-analysis shows vaginal progesterone reduces preterm birth and neonatal morbidity in twins with a cervix under 25 mm, whereas routine cerclage and bed rest are ineffective or harmful.
questions.reference: DC Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics 9e, Ch. Multiple Pregnancy

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: In a twin delivery, the first twin delivers vaginally as a vertex and the second is transverse with intact membranes. The appropriate action is:
options: Internal podalic version and breech extraction, or external cephalic version, by an experienced operator
Immediate caesarean section in all cases
questions.concept: With the cervix fully dilated and the uterus relaxed, the second twin can usually be delivered by version and breech extraction under continuous monitoring, avoiding a combined vaginal and abdominal delivery.
questions.reference: DC Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics 9e, Ch. Multiple Pregnancy

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: Which mechanism explains twin reversed arterial perfusion sequence?
options: An acardiac twin is perfused retrogradely through artery-to-artery anastomoses by the pump twin
questions.concept: Deoxygenated blood flowing backwards into the acardiac mass causes it to grow abnormally while imposing a high-output load on the pump twin, so cord occlusion of the acardiac twin is offered.
questions.reference: DC Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics 9e, Ch. Multiple Pregnancy

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: Monoamniotic twins are delivered by planned caesarean at about 32 to 34 weeks primarily because of:
options: The risk of sudden fetal death from cord entanglement
questions.concept: With no dividing membrane, cords intertwine in nearly all monoamniotic pregnancies and can knot acutely, so inpatient surveillance and early planned delivery are standard.
questions.reference: DC Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics 9e, Ch. Multiple Pregnancy

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: Which physiological change of pregnancy most increases the risk of failed intubation at caesarean section?
options: Airway oedema with increased Mallampati grade and large breasts
questions.concept: Capillary engorgement narrows the airway and progresses through labour, and combined with a short neck and enlarged breasts makes laryngoscopy harder, so a smaller tube and a ramped position are used.
questions.reference: DC Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics 9e, Ch. Obstetric Analgesia and Maternal Mortality

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: Why is a pregnant woman at increased risk of aspiration during general anaesthesia?
options: Progesterone-induced relaxation of the lower oesophageal sphincter with raised intragastric pressure
questions.concept: These changes underlie Mendelson syndrome, which is why regional anaesthesia is preferred and why acid prophylaxis, cricoid pressure and rapid sequence induction are used when general anaesthesia is unavoidable.
questions.reference: DC Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics 9e, Ch. Obstetric Analgesia and Maternal Mortality

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: In a district recording 24 maternal deaths against 40000 live births in a year, the maternal mortality ratio is:
questions.concept: The ratio is maternal deaths divided by live births multiplied by 100000, so 24 divided by 40000 gives 60 per 100000; the denominator of live births is what distinguishes the ratio from the maternal mortality rate.
questions.reference: DC Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics 9e, Ch. Obstetric Analgesia and Maternal Mortality

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A woman receives an epidural in labour and 10 minutes later has a rapidly ascending block with hypotension, difficulty breathing and weak arms. The diagnosis is:
options: Inadvertent intrathecal injection causing a high or total spinal block
questions.concept: A total spinal requires immediate airway support, ventilation, fluids and vasopressors; a test dose and incremental administration are designed to detect misplacement before a full dose is given.
questions.reference: DC Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics 9e, Ch. Obstetric Analgesia and Maternal Mortality

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: Which drug is used first for hypotension after spinal anaesthesia for caesarean section, and why?
options: Phenylephrine, because it maintains uterine perfusion better than ephedrine and causes less fetal acidosis
Ephedrine, because it is a direct agonist
Adrenaline, because of its inotropic action
questions.concept: Ephedrine crosses the placenta and increases fetal metabolic rate and acidaemia, so a pure alpha agonist with left lateral tilt and fluid co-loading is now preferred.
questions.reference: DC Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics 9e, Ch. Obstetric Analgesia and Maternal Mortality

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: Which category of maternal death is classed as a direct obstetric death?
options: Death from pre-existing rheumatic heart disease aggravated by pregnancy
Death in a road traffic accident during pregnancy
Death from tuberculosis diagnosed in pregnancy
questions.concept: Direct deaths result from obstetric complications of pregnancy, labour or the puerperium; aggravated pre-existing disease is an indirect death and accidents are incidental or coincidental deaths.
questions.reference: DC Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics 9e, Ch. Obstetric Analgesia and Maternal Mortality

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: Which regional technique is preferred for a woman needing urgent caesarean section who already has a working labour epidural?
questions.concept: Extending an existing block is faster and avoids the risks of both general anaesthesia and a second neuraxial puncture, provided the epidural has been providing good analgesia.
questions.reference: DC Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics 9e, Ch. Obstetric Analgesia and Maternal Mortality

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A woman collapses shortly after delivery with hypoxia, hypotension, seizures and profound coagulopathy. The likely diagnosis and initial management are:
options: Amniotic fluid embolism, managed by immediate cardiorespiratory support and aggressive correction of coagulopathy
questions.concept: Amniotic fluid embolism is a clinical diagnosis of exclusion presenting with the triad of hypoxia, hypotension and disseminated intravascular coagulation, and there is no specific treatment beyond intensive supportive care.
questions.reference: DC Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics 9e, Ch. Obstetric Analgesia and Maternal Mortality

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: Which change to the definition of a maternal death captures deaths occurring between 42 days and one year after delivery?
questions.concept: Recognising late maternal deaths matters because suicide, cardiac disease and cancer contribute substantially to mortality beyond the traditional 42-day window used in maternal mortality ratios.
questions.reference: DC Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics 9e, Ch. Obstetric Analgesia and Maternal Mortality

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Physiological changes in pregnancy & fetal development
questions.stem: Which haematological change explains the physiological anaemia of pregnancy?
options: Plasma volume rises proportionately more than red cell mass, diluting haemoglobin
questions.concept: Plasma volume rises by about 45 percent and red cell mass by only 20 to 30 percent, so haemoglobin concentration falls even though total oxygen-carrying capacity increases.
questions.reference: DC Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics 9e, Ch. Physiological Changes in Pregnancy

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Physiological changes in pregnancy & fetal development
questions.stem: Systemic vascular resistance in normal pregnancy:
options: Falls, producing a mid-trimester nadir in blood pressure
Falls only in the third trimester
questions.concept: Progesterone and placental vasodilators reduce resistance from early pregnancy, so blood pressure dips around 20 to 24 weeks and returns to baseline by term, which can mask chronic hypertension at booking.
questions.reference: DC Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics 9e, Ch. Physiological Changes in Pregnancy

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Physiological changes in pregnancy & fetal development
questions.stem: Which respiratory change is characteristic of normal pregnancy?
options: Increased tidal volume with unchanged respiratory rate, giving a mild respiratory alkalosis
Increased respiratory rate with unchanged tidal volume
questions.concept: Progesterone-driven hyperventilation lowers arterial carbon dioxide to about 30 mmHg with renal bicarbonate compensation, which facilitates transfer of fetal carbon dioxide across the placenta.
questions.reference: DC Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics 9e, Ch. Physiological Changes in Pregnancy

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Physiological changes in pregnancy & fetal development
questions.stem: Which renal change makes a serum creatinine of 1.0 mg/dL abnormal in pregnancy?
options: Glomerular filtration rate rises by about 50 percent, so normal creatinine falls to about 0.4 to 0.8 mg/dL
questions.concept: Because filtration rises so much, a creatinine within the non-pregnant reference range may signify significant renal impairment, which is why pregnancy-specific ranges must be used.
questions.reference: DC Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics 9e, Ch. Physiological Changes in Pregnancy

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Physiological changes in pregnancy & fetal development
questions.stem: Which change in the coagulation system of pregnancy explains the increased thrombotic risk?
options: Rises in fibrinogen and factors VII, VIII and X with a fall in protein S and increased plasminogen activator inhibitor
questions.concept: Pregnancy is a physiologically hypercoagulable state that limits bleeding at delivery, but combined with venous stasis and endothelial injury it fulfils Virchow's triad, so thromboprophylaxis is risk-assessed at every admission.
questions.reference: DC Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics 9e, Ch. Physiological Changes in Pregnancy

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Physiological changes in pregnancy & fetal development
questions.stem: Which gastrointestinal change of pregnancy accounts for constipation and gallstone formation?
options: Progesterone-mediated smooth muscle relaxation slowing transit and reducing gallbladder emptying
questions.concept: Reduced motility prolongs colonic water absorption and allows biliary stasis with more lithogenic bile, so gallstones and cholestasis are commoner in pregnancy and the puerperium.
questions.reference: DC Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics 9e, Ch. Physiological Changes in Pregnancy

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Physiological changes in pregnancy & fetal development
questions.stem: At what gestation does the fetal kidney begin to contribute the major part of amniotic fluid, making fluid volume a marker of renal function?
questions.concept: Before 16 weeks amniotic fluid is largely a transudate, after which fetal urine dominates, which is why bilateral renal agenesis produces anhydramnios in the second trimester with Potter sequence.
questions.reference: DC Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics 9e, Ch. Physiological Changes in Pregnancy

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Physiological changes in pregnancy & fetal development
questions.stem: Which fetal circulatory shunt closes functionally within minutes of birth as a result of rising arterial oxygen tension?
questions.concept: Oxygen constricts ductal smooth muscle while the fall in circulating prostaglandin E2 after placental separation removes the dilating stimulus, which is why prostaglandin synthesis inhibitors close a patent duct and prostaglandin infusion keeps it open.
questions.reference: DC Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics 9e, Ch. Physiological Changes in Pregnancy

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Physiological changes in pregnancy & fetal development
questions.stem: Which substance crosses the placenta by simple diffusion and is therefore transferred at a rate limited by uterine blood flow rather than by carrier availability?
questions.concept: Oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse down their gradients so their transfer is flow-limited, glucose crosses by facilitated diffusion, amino acids by active transport and IgG by receptor-mediated endocytosis.
questions.reference: DC Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics 9e, Ch. Physiological Changes in Pregnancy

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: Which of the four Ts accounts for about 70 percent of primary postpartum haemorrhage?
questions.concept: Because atony predominates, active management of the third stage with a prophylactic uterotonic is the single most effective preventive measure and reduces haemorrhage by about 60 percent.
questions.reference: DC Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics 9e, Ch. Postpartum Haemorrhage

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: Which drug given within 3 hours of onset reduces death due to bleeding in postpartum haemorrhage?
questions.concept: The WOMAN trial showed reduced death from bleeding when tranexamic acid was given early, with no increase in thrombotic events, so it is now part of standard first-line management alongside uterotonics.
questions.reference: DC Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics 9e, Ch. Postpartum Haemorrhage

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: Which uterotonic is contraindicated in a woman with asthma?
questions.concept: Carboprost is a prostaglandin F2-alpha analogue that causes bronchospasm, whereas methylergometrine is avoided in hypertension and oxytocin in large rapid boluses because of hypotension and water retention.
questions.reference: DC Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics 9e, Ch. Postpartum Haemorrhage

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: After delivery of the placenta the uterus is well contracted but bright red bleeding continues. The next step is:
options: Systematic examination of the cervix, vagina and perineum under good light for trauma
questions.concept: With a contracted uterus the cause is genital tract trauma, so a careful inspection with adequate exposure and analgesia identifies cervical or high vaginal tears that would not respond to uterotonics.
questions.reference: DC Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics 9e, Ch. Postpartum Haemorrhage

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A woman has continuing atonic haemorrhage despite uterotonics. Which balloon-based measure is used before laparotomy?
questions.concept: A hydrostatic balloon achieves tamponade in about 85 percent of atonic cases, is quick and preserves fertility, and its failure is a useful trigger for moving to laparotomy.
questions.reference: DC Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics 9e, Ch. Postpartum Haemorrhage

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: Which compression suture is used at laparotomy for atonic postpartum haemorrhage?
questions.concept: The brace suture compresses the anterior and posterior uterine walls together, and variants such as Hayman and Cho square sutures serve the same purpose; the other options are cervical cerclage techniques.
questions.reference: DC Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics 9e, Ch. Postpartum Haemorrhage

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: Secondary postpartum haemorrhage at 10 days with a tender bulky uterus and offensive lochia is most often due to:
options: Endometritis with retained products of conception
questions.concept: Treatment is antibiotics with gentle evacuation once infection is controlled, and ultrasound helps but cannot always distinguish clot from retained tissue.
questions.reference: DC Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics 9e, Ch. Postpartum Haemorrhage

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: A woman with placenta praevia and a previous caesarean has bleeding at caesarean from the lower segment which does not respond to oxytocin. Why is this bleeding hard to control?
options: The lower segment has less myometrium and contracts poorly, so mechanical or surgical measures are needed
Oxytocin receptors are absent in pregnancy
The uterine arteries are absent in the lower segment
questions.concept: Lower-segment atony after praevia is a recognised cause of intractable haemorrhage, addressed by local sutures, balloon tamponade, vessel ligation or hysterectomy rather than by more uterotonic.
questions.reference: DC Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics 9e, Ch. Postpartum Haemorrhage

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: Which intervention is definitive when postpartum haemorrhage persists despite uterotonics, tamponade, compression sutures and vessel ligation?
questions.concept: Deciding on hysterectomy early enough is what saves lives, and delay while repeating failed measures is a recurrent theme in maternal mortality reviews.
questions.reference: DC Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics 9e, Ch. Postpartum Haemorrhage

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: Which late complication follows severe postpartum haemorrhage with prolonged hypotension and presents with failure of lactation and amenorrhoea?
questions.concept: The enlarged, portally supplied anterior pituitary of pregnancy is vulnerable to ischaemic necrosis, so panhypopituitarism follows, typically declaring itself first as failure of lactation.
questions.reference: DC Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics 9e, Ch. Postpartum Haemorrhage
